title.em: then check it in working code.

approach.body: I look for where automation or an interface loses people's trust, design clear ways to refuse and recover, and test those choices early in running software or hardware prototypes rather than static slides.

1.b: Find where people hesitate, misclick, or stop trusting an automated workflow.

2.b: Skip the flashy shortcut when an explicit confirmation, or simply leaving a field blank, is what protects the user.

3.b: Build working Next.js, Electron, browser extension, or ESP32 prototypes with automated tests behind them.

4.b: Keep what was checked on the device or in the repo separate from testing with outside participants, which is still to be done.

designPrinciples.title: Friction First
designPrinciples.description: Start from real failure modes, false-positive costs, and broken user expectations before drawing components.

designPrinciples.title: Falsify Early
designPrinciples.description: Ship working firmware, extensions, or UI state machines early so brittle assumptions break in testing rather than shipping.

designPrinciples.title: Accessible & Tactile
designPrinciples.description: Keyboard flow, >= 24px targets, AAA typography contrast, and 0ms reduced-motion parity belong in the spec from day one.

designPrinciples.title: Calibrated Evidence
designPrinciples.description: Separate bench checks and synthetic runs from cohort studies; state every unverified limit plainly.

headline.text: I design interactions that help people stay oriented.

about.p1: I'm finishing my Master of Interaction Design at The University of Queensland in November 2026 after earning a BSc (Hons) in Computer Science (2:1) at Swansea University in Wales. Training in both engineering and design keeps me realistic about what software and hardware can actually handle once latency, permissions, and tired users come into play.
about.p2: My work sits where people meet complex systems: AI tools that act beyond what users are confident about, multiplayer hardware that pulls people out of solo silence, and workflows that hide failures or privacy risks. Rather than stopping at static slides, I build working prototypes in TypeScript, Electron, Chrome extensions, or ESP32 C++, so a rule can visibly fail and then be revised.
about.p3: In AI-assisted builds I am clear about what I own: the human tension, the shortcuts that were rejected, the limits on when the product refuses, and the acceptance checks on real hardware or in Playwright. I treat generated code as a draft to check, not as correct by default.
about.p4: If you have a complex interaction problem or a graduate opening, write to me and I'll get back to you quickly.

1.b: If a study never challenges a design choice, it didn't earn its time.

2.b: The best interaction gets out of the way so people can act with confidence.

3.b: Empty states, recovery paths, and physical confirmations are where trust is actually won or lost.

4.b: Writing down constraints and assumptions keeps everyone aligned long after a meeting ends.
